candidate.answerReason: Counting by the integer coordinate of the left edge gives 6, 15, 17, and 12 squares, totaling 50.

methods.label: Count by the left edge
methods.explanation:
An axis-parallel square with integer vertices has an integer side length. Let its bottom-left vertex be \((i,b)\) and its side length be the positive integer \(k\).

The triangular region satisfies \(y\ge-0.1\), \(x\le5.1\), and \(y\le\pi x\). Integer vertices must therefore have \(y\ge0\) and \(0\le x\le5\). Because the sloping boundary rises to the right, the top-left corner is the most restrictive point of the square for that boundary. Thus containment is equivalent to
\[
b\ge0,\qquad i+k\le5,\qquad b+k\le\pi i.
\]
The case \(i=0\) is impossible because \(b+k>0\), so \(i\) can only be \(1,2,3,4\).

Let \(H_i=\lfloor\pi i\rfloor\), the greatest integer at most \(\pi i\). Using \(3<\pi<13/4\), we obtain
\[
H_1=3,\quad H_2=6,\quad H_3=9,\quad H_4=12.
\]
For fixed \(i\) and \(k\), the bottom coordinate can be any integer from \(0\) through \(H_i-k\), giving \(H_i-k+1\) squares. The allowable side lengths satisfy both \(k\le5-i\) and \(k\le H_i\). Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
i=1 &: \quad 3+2+1=6,\\
i=2 &: \quad 6+5+4=15,\\
i=3 &: \quad 9+8=17,\\
i=4 &: \quad 12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every valid square has exactly one left coordinate, side length, and bottom coordinate, so these cases include every square exactly once. The total is
\[
6+15+17+12=\boxed{50},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
